title: History of Political Philosophy
author: Leo Strauss and Joseph Cropsey
notes: Primarily just read the first chapter. I was interested in the claim that the Republic was proto-communist. It's really well structured and a great read.

title: Philosophy and Real Politics
author: Guess
notes: Interesting take on Kant and 'realpolitik'. I have not read anything in that regard since my old professor.

title: The Trial and Death Of Socrates
author: Plato
notes: Always a fun read, have not looked into it since college. A really enjoyable rhetoric.

title: The Culture Struggle
author: Parenti
notes: I have not read Parenti in years (RIP). I think his work was interesting as a short Marxist critique. There's lots to take away from this if you want a short read.

title: Antigone
author: Sophocles
notes: A wonderful classic. I have not read this book since Prof. Kiel passed away in 2013. He was one of the few people who worked through this as an act of defiance and it's context.

title: Antigone
author: Zizek
notes: A really goofy retelling. I do not know that I walked away processing anything beyond it.

title: Existentialism as a humanism
author: Sartre
notes: I think what I enjoyed the most out of this book is embracing the weight of a choice or lack. The writing is light and the exchange at the end of the book is a wonderful antagonism between two systems.

title: A Bitter Trial: Evelyn Waugh and John Carmel Cardinal Heenan on Liturgical Changes
author: Waugh and Heenan
notes: This book was really interesting to read. Short and brief, it contextualises the difference between taking church serious and what I feel has eventually become an overstimulation and aesthetic overdrive of church (Think megachurches down south).

title: America
author: Ronell
notes: My first book by Avita Ronell. I remember seeing her give an intro to Zizek multiple times and wanted to always read her works. I feel like I wasted my time. It feels more like poetry without aim rather than a critique. There's nowhere to go or grow with her work, and it feels like in part it's because of the structures she builds for herself.

title: The Society of the Spectacle
author: Debord
notes: While I don't agree with some of it, and some of it comes across as lofty or poetic, I still enjoy this book. There's some line between Reality, Fiction and Ideology that it does a good job of pointing to. In the face of an increasingly online world choked by images and assumed meaning, this book is still worth re-evaluation.

title: Gyo
author: Ito
notes: Wonderful retelling of ww2 era Japanese horror and social trauma. It does such a good job of painting body horror.

title: Haunted Houses
author: Roberts
notes: Fun stories around haunted houses in the US. A wonderful exchange and cool look into American history and folklore.

title: Twilight of the Machines
author: Zerzan
notes: Read this to my daughter at bedtime. She will only have one experience at presymbolic existance and I might as well lull her to sleep with what life could be like. It's a wonderful collection of Zerzan's works, and it makes me appreciate his consistency over the years.

title: Uzumeki
author: Ito
notes: Wonderful. An amazing horror based around something that is mundane and nauseating. Body horror, folklore and a lack of closure. It is an amazing peak into social trauma and memetics in a way.

title: Smashed
author: Ito
notes: The one that stuck with me most out of this collection was around the vampire which was a story about an eating disorder. It's such a wonderful exlporation of the morbid.

title: The Revolution of Everyday Life
author: Vaneigem
notes: Amazing and great peak into Situationism. A beautiful experience re-thinking what life could potentially be like, and the mundaneness of everyday.
